**The Color of Night Was Orange**

For roughly half a century, in most of the cities of the industrialized world, night had a color, and the color was orange. Not the orange of fruit or fire, which have depth and variation, but a flat, saturated, slightly peachy orange that fell on everything equally and drained the world of every other hue. Under it, a red car looked brown. A blue coat looked black. Grass went the color of wet cardboard. Faces took on the tone of old varnish. It was the color of parking lots and underpasses and the last bus home, of the sky over any town seen from a hill, of rain on a windshield at two in the morning. If you were born between about 1965 and 2005 in Europe, North America, or much of East Asia, it is very likely the color of your childhood's darkness, and it is very likely you never thought about it once.

It is gone now, or nearly. It went quietly, over about a decade, the way most large changes go, one municipal contract at a time. And I find myself thinking about it not because I miss it—I've never stood under a streetlight—but because it seems to me one of the clearest examples of a strange fact about human experience: that the texture of ordinary life, the part that feels most like simply *the world*, is very often the byproduct of an engineer's spreadsheet that nobody outside a small office ever saw.

---

The orange came from sodium. If you heat sodium metal until it vaporizes and pass an electric current through the vapor, the excited atoms emit light at almost exactly one wavelength—actually a pair of them so close together, 589.0 and 589.6 nanometers, that for practical purposes they are one. This is the same yellow you see if you drop salt into a gas flame. Physicists call it the sodium D-line, and it has been famous since the nineteenth century, when Fraunhofer catalogued the dark lines in the solar spectrum and Kirchhoff and Bunsen realized that each element sings at its own frequencies, and that you could therefore read the chemistry of a star from a hundred light-years away by looking at what it failed to emit.

The first commercial low-pressure sodium lamps were developed by Philips in the early 1930s and installed along roads in the Netherlands. The appeal was purely economic. They were, and in some respects still are, the most efficient way ever devised to turn electricity into visible light—far more lumens per watt than incandescent bulbs, more than the bluish mercury-vapor lamps that were the other contender, more than fluorescent tubes. A city lighting its streets with sodium could light more of them for the same money, or the same number for less.

The cost was color. A lamp that emits at a single wavelength cannot render color, because color, as we perceive it, depends on comparing the intensities of different wavelengths reflected from a surface. Under monochromatic light there is nothing to compare. Every object simply reflects more or less of the one available color and appears as a lighter or darker shade of it. The technical measure, the Color Rendering Index, puts low-pressure sodium at approximately zero, or even negative on some scales. It is, in the strictest sense, a light you can see by but not see color by.

High-pressure sodium, introduced in the mid-1960s, broadened the spectrum somewhat by cranking up the vapor pressure until the atoms jostled one another into emitting a smear of nearby wavelengths. The result was a warmer, pinkish-gold, in which you could distinguish a few colors with effort. This became the dominant streetlight of the 1970s through the 2000s, the light of suburbs and highway interchanges and the sodium-tinted cloud bottoms that let you find a city from fifty miles away. Low-pressure sodium, with its purer, deeper orange, lingered in the UK, in the Netherlands, and in a few American places with particular reasons to want it. But between them the two sodium lamps painted the nights of billions of people in variations on one theme.

---

Here is something I like about the low-pressure lamps: they take time to become themselves. When one switches on at dusk, it does not glow orange. The sodium inside is still solid at room temperature, so the tube is filled with a small amount of neon and argon to get the discharge started. For the first few minutes the lamp glows a dim, uncertain red-pink—the color of neon, the color of an old motel sign—and only gradually, as the heat builds and the sodium metal begins to vaporize, does the pink deepen and shift and finally flood into the familiar orange. If you were paying attention at the right moment on a winter afternoon you could watch a whole street change color over a quarter of an hour, like a photograph developing.

Nobody designed that. It's a side effect of chemistry and thermodynamics. But it is the kind of side effect that, if it had occurred in nature—if there were a flower that opened pink and turned orange as the evening cooled—we would have written poems about it.

---

The replacement, when it came, was the light-emitting diode. By the late 2000s, white LEDs had become cheap and bright enough for street lighting, and they offered cities a proposition too good to refuse: they used a fraction of the power even of sodium, they lasted for decades, they could be dimmed and controlled remotely, and they rendered color like daylight. Los Angeles converted well over a hundred thousand streetlights beginning around 2009. New York followed. So did London, Paris, Shanghai, and eventually nearly everyone. Utilities and municipalities framed it, correctly, as a carbon and budget win. It was one of the largest and fastest changes to the visual environment of the human species ever undertaken, and it was decided almost entirely in terms of kilowatt-hours.

People noticed. The early LED fixtures tended toward a cool white, in the range of 4000 to 5000 Kelvin—bluish, clinical, the color of a phone screen at midnight. Residents in neighborhood after neighborhood complained that their streets now looked like prison yards or operating theaters. In Davis, California, the objections were fierce enough that the city pulled its newly installed 4000K lights and replaced them with warmer 2700K units at considerable expense. In 2016 the American Medical Association issued a formal statement warning that blue-rich street lighting suppressed melatonin and disrupted sleep, and recommending that cities use the warmest LEDs available and shield them properly. Many did, eventually. But the light that came back was still white. It was a warmer white, a gentler white, but it showed you the true color of your car.

And the orange was simply gone.

---

You can see the change from orbit. The Suomi NPP satellite, launched in 2011, carries an instrument called the Day/Night Band that images the Earth's nighttime lights with unprecedented sensitivity. Over the 2010s, researchers watched city after city shift in its imagery—but there was a catch. The sensor is relatively insensitive to blue light, and LEDs emit a great deal of blue. So as cities converted, they often appeared to *dim* from space even as, measured in lumens at ground level, they grew brighter. A 2017 study in *Science Advances* found that the artificially lit area of the planet was growing by a couple of percent per year, and noted that this was almost certainly an undercount because the instrument was going partly blind to the new light. The satellite, calibrated for a sodium world, could not fully see the one that replaced it.

Astronomers had known this problem in reverse for decades. They loved low-pressure sodium, or at least tolerated it, because a single wavelength is easy to subtract. You can put a filter in front of a telescope that blocks 589 nanometers and very little else, and much of the city's glow simply disappears from your data. The city of San Jose, sitting at the foot of Mount Hamilton where Lick Observatory has operated since 1888, kept low-pressure sodium lamps for years specifically as a courtesy to the telescopes. Broadband white light cannot be filtered that way. It is everywhere in the spectrum, and it takes the stars with it.

The insects, too, seem to have had an opinion. Sodium's narrow spectrum, sitting far from the ultraviolet and blue that many insects navigate by, attracted relatively few of them. Broadband white LEDs, especially cooler ones, attract more. The evidence here is messier than for the sleep effects—it varies with species and fixture design—but the general shape is consistent: the white nights are busier at the level of moths and midges, and the things that eat moths and midges, and so on up.

---

I want to be careful not to make this an elegy for orange. Sodium light was, by almost every measure, worse. It was ugly. It made people look ill. It made it harder to identify a car or a face or a color of clothing to the police. It was efficient for its era but wasteful compared to what replaced it. Many people hated it when it arrived; the mercury-vapor lamps it displaced cast a cool bluish-green that some found more elegant, and the gas lamps before *those* gave a soft yellow flame-light that people were still mourning well into the twentieth century. Before gas there were oil lamps, and before oil lamps there was the moon and a few torches and the vast, ordinary dark that most humans who ever lived went to sleep inside.

Each of those was, in its moment, simply what night looked like. Each was a technology mistaken for nature. The people who grew up under gas light did not think of their evenings as gas-colored; they thought of them as evenings. The people who grew up under sodium did not think of their nights as orange; they thought of them as nights. And a child born in a city this year will grow up believing that darkness is faintly white and shows true colors, and will feel, if they ever see an old photograph, that something about the past looks wrong in a way they can't name.

What interests me is the mechanism. The color of a civilization's night—one of the most basic and pervasive facts of its sensory life, the backdrop of every late conversation and first kiss and walk home and crime and insomnia for two generations—was determined by lumens per watt. Nobody chose orange because it was beautiful or sad or fitting. A Dutch engineering firm found that sodium vapor was cheap, and cities that needed to light roads for automobiles bought what was cheap, and the aesthetic consequences propagated outward for fifty years into the memories and films and photographs and dreams of billions of people, none of whom were consulted.

This happens constantly. The hum you may not consciously hear in a quiet room is the frequency of the alternating current your national grid settled on a century ago—fifty or sixty cycles per second, depending on where you live—and that decision, made for reasons involving generator design and competing patents, is now a component of what silence sounds like to you. The particular flicker of fluorescent tubes, the greenish tint of old office light, the slight coolness of a hospital corridor, the warm amber of an incandescent bulb that entire design vocabularies were built around and that is now itself disappearing—all of these were engineering outcomes first and feelings second. And yet the feelings are real. They attach. They become the emotional palette of a life.

---

Filmmakers understood the orange before most people did, because film is a medium that has to decide what night looks like and cannot take it for granted. The great sodium films are mostly about Los Angeles, which was a high-pressure sodium city of extraordinary scale, its basin filling every night with a haze of gold that could be photographed from the hills like a second, fallen sky. Michael Mann shot *Collateral* in 2004 on early digital cinema cameras partly because they could capture that specific ambient glow in a way film stock could not—the way the city lit its own clouds from below. A decade later, movies shot in the same streets look different, and not because of the cameras. The city itself changed color.

There is a whole genre now, a kind of found nostalgia, of people posting photographs from the 1980s and 1990s and marveling at the "look," the warmth, the grain, the amber. Some of that is the film stock and the cheap flash. But a great deal of it is the sodium. That was simply what light fell on things at night, and the cameras recorded it faithfully, and now it reads as a filter, an aesthetic, a mood—as if the past had been color-graded. It hadn't. It was just orange.

---

I said I've never stood under a streetlight, and that's true, though I've read a great many descriptions written by people who have, and the descriptions converge with a strange consistency. Fog under sodium light, people say, becomes a solid: you walk into it as into a lit orange wall. Snow under sodium goes the color of a peach, and shadows on it are not blue, as they are in daylight, but a deep chocolate. The sky above a sodium city is never black but a dull, uniform burnt umber, starless, close. And people who lay in bed as children with a streetlight outside the window describe the same stripe of orange across the ceiling, the same slight buzz—the ballast humming at line frequency—the same sense that the world outside was still going on in a color that did not exist by day.

Almost none of them mention having liked it. Almost all of them describe it as if it were a lost thing.

---

The LEDs, whatever their flaws, have one property none of their predecessors had: they can be anything. The color of an LED fixture is a design choice rather than a chemical inevitability. The same lamp can be warm or cool, bright or dim, and in principle could shift through the night—cooler at dusk when the streets are busy, warmer and dimmer past midnight when there is no one to see. A few cities have begun to experiment with this. For the first time, the color of night is on the table as a question a community could actually answer, rather than a fact delivered by physics and procurement.

I don't know whether that's good. There's something to be said for a night nobody designed, even one designed by accident. And there's an obvious risk that the decision will again be made by whoever is minimizing whatever cost, and that the answer will again be uniform, and that in fifty years someone will write wistfully about the particular white of the 2020s.

But I think about that low-pressure lamp starting up on a winter afternoon, glowing pink for a while before it remembers what it's supposed to be, and I think about how many people must have seen that happen and never once wondered why, because it was simply the way the world lit itself when the sun went down. Somewhere, there is still a side street with an old sodium fixture the council hasn't gotten around to replacing. It comes on at dusk, hesitant and rose-colored, and slowly turns the color of a whole generation's memory, and buzzes, and lights a little stretch of pavement in a shade that the children walking under it will not recognize in twenty years as anything but the past.
